listeningParts.title: Booking a glass-blowing class
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a glass studio to book a beginners' glass-blowing session.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good morning, Furnace Lane Glass Studio, Niamh speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I'm calling about your glass-blowing taster sessions. I saw a leaflet in the library, and I'd like to book one as a birthday present for my sister.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: What a lovely idea. The taster sessions are for complete beginners. They last two and a half hours, and each person works one-to-one with one of our glass artists at the furnace. Was there a particular date you had in mind?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Her birthday's on the twelfth, which is a Friday, so ideally that day.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Let me check. I'm afraid Friday the twelfth is fully booked. But we do have places on Saturday the thirteenth, in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Saturday's fine, actually. She doesn't work at weekends, and it means we can go out for lunch together afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Great. And how many people would that be for?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Well, originally I was thinking of four: me, my sister, her husband and my nephew. How old do people have to be?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The minimum age is sixteen, I'm afraid. It's because of the temperatures involved: the furnace runs at over a thousand degrees, and our insurance doesn't cover younger participants.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ah, my nephew's only fourteen, so he'll have to wait a couple of years. So it'll be three of us, then.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Three people on Saturday morning. Now, the price. On weekdays, it's fifty-five pounds per person, but weekend sessions are sixty-eight pounds, because they're so popular.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's okay. What does that include?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It includes all the materials, the tuition, and a hot drink when you arrive. And everyone makes their own piece to take home. For beginners, that's a paperweight. You choose your colours, and the artist helps you gather the molten glass and shape it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A paperweight. That sounds perfect. Can we take it home straight away?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No, and that surprises a lot of people. If hot glass cools too quickly, it develops stresses inside, and it can crack, sometimes days later. So all the finished pieces go into a kiln overnight, where they cool down very slowly. You can collect them from the studio any time after midday the next day, or we can post them to you for a fee of six pounds.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll come and collect them. Will there be time to watch the artists working, too?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes. At the end of the session, one of our artists gives a short demonstration, usually making a vase or a bowl, and explains what's happening to the glass at each stage. People find it fascinating, because the glass changes colour as it cools, from bright orange to its real colour. There's also a small shop where you can buy work made by our resident artists.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. Is there anything we should wear?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, this is important. Please wear clothes made of cotton, or another natural fibre like wool. Synthetic fabrics, such as polyester or nylon, can melt if a spark lands on them. Long trousers are best, and no loose scarves.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Got it. What about shoes?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Closed shoes, please, ideally leather boots. Sandals and open-toed shoes aren't allowed in the hot shop under any circumstances. We provide safety glasses, so you don't need to bring those.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. And is there parking nearby?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's no parking at the studio itself, but there's a free car park behind the library, which is about three minutes' walk away. On Saturdays, it can fill up by ten, so try to arrive early.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's useful, thanks. Shall I give you my details?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Please. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Ashworth. A-S-H-W-O-R-T-H.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Ashworth. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh seven seven oh oh, nine one two, four eight three.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. I'll send you a confirmation email with directions and a short safety form that each of you needs to sign. Payment is due when you arrive. And if your sister enjoys it, we also run a four-week evening course for people who want to take it further.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll let her know. Thanks so much for your help.

listeningParts.title: Inside a recycling plant
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide talks to a group of residents visiting a materials recovery facility.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Greenvale Materials Recovery Facility. I'm Joel, and I'll be showing you around this morning. Before we go onto the viewing platform, where it's very noisy, I'd like to explain what happens here and give you some tips that will make our job a lot easier.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Everything that you put in your household recycling bin ends up in this building. We receive about three hundred tonnes of material on an average weekday, and our job is to separate it into streams of paper, cardboard, metals, glass and different types of plastic, which are then sold to manufacturers who turn them into new products.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Let's start with plastics, because that's where most of the confusion lies. You'll have noticed that many plastic items have a small triangle printed on them with a number inside, from one to seven. A lot of people assume that the triangle means the item can be recycled, but that's not actually the case. The number simply tells you what type of plastic the item is made of. Number one, for example, is PET, which is used for most drinks bottles, and number two is high-density polyethylene, which is used for milk bottles and many shampoo bottles. Both of those are easy for us to recycle. Others, such as number three, PVC, are much harder.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: So how do we sort everything? First, the material passes over a series of rotating screens, which separate flat items like paper from three-dimensional ones like bottles and cans. Then powerful magnets lift out the steel cans. Aluminium isn't magnetic, so it's removed further along by a machine that creates a changing magnetic field, which actually pushes the cans off the belt.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The plastics are sorted by optical sorters. These shine infrared light onto each item, and because each type of plastic reflects the light in a slightly different way, the machine can identify it, and then a precisely timed jet of air blows it into the right container. It's remarkably fast. The one exception is black plastic, like the trays that meat often comes in. The black colouring absorbs the infrared light, so the sorters simply can't see it, and it ends up being sent for disposal. So if you can avoid buying food in black trays, please do.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, some tips. The biggest problem we face is contamination, meaning things in the recycling that shouldn't be there, or recyclable items covered in food. Containers do need to be empty and reasonably clean, but you don't need to scrub them or use hot water. A quick rinse in your washing-up water is enough.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Please don't put plastic bags or other soft plastics in your bin. They wrap themselves around the rotating screens, and we have to stop the whole line several times a day so that staff can cut them free. Most large supermarkets now have collection points for soft plastics, including carrier bags and bread bags, so take them there instead.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Shampoo bottles and cleaning product bottles are fine in your household bin, but please put the lids back on, because loose lids are too small for our machines and fall through the screens. Black meat trays should go in your general rubbish, for the reason I explained.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And, most importantly, never put batteries in any of your bins. Lithium batteries from phones, toys and electronic cigarettes can be crushed or punctured in the collection lorry or here on the line, and when that happens, they can catch fire. We have small fires here more often than you'd think. The same goes for old mobile phones and other broken electrical items: please take those to the household waste site on Mill Road, which has special containers for them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Right, if everyone could put on a high-visibility vest and a pair of ear defenders, we'll head up to the platform.

listeningParts.title: A project on natural dyes
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two chemistry students, Priya and Tom, discuss their natural dye experiments with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, Priya, Tom. So, you've finished the practical work for your natural dyes project. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Really well, on the whole. As you know, we wanted to compare how well different natural dyes work on wool and cotton, and how resistant the colours are to light.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We deliberately chose dye sources from the kitchen, things that are cheap and usually just thrown away: onion skins, avocado stones and the outer leaves of red cabbage. We also used turmeric, which isn't waste, of course, but it's widely available and gives a really strong yellow.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how did you prepare the fibres?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We treated all the samples with alum first, as a mordant. It helps the dye molecules bind to the fibres. Then we simmered them in the dye baths for an hour. We kept the temperature just below ninety degrees, because boiling can damage wool fibres and make them felt together.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Sensible. What were the colours like?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The onion skins gave a lovely golden orange, and the turmeric a very bright yellow. The surprise was the avocado stones. We'd expected brown, but they produced a soft pink colour, which was beautiful.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Yes, people are often surprised by that. Did the wool and cotton behave differently?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Very differently. The wool took up far more colour than the cotton with every dye. Some of the cotton samples were so pale they were hardly coloured at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's what I'd expect. Wool is a protein fibre, and natural dyes generally bond much more readily with protein than with cellulose, which is what cotton is made of. Traditional dyers often treated cotton with tannins first, from oak bark, for example, to help the dye attach. You might try that if you have time, or at least discuss it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We will. Then for the light test, we put a set of samples on a south-facing windowsill, with half of each sample covered by card, so we could compare the exposed and protected parts. We'd planned to leave them for three weeks, but the weather was so cloudy that we extended it to four.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good thinking. And which dye was least resistant to light?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Turmeric, by far. It started off the brightest, but after four weeks the exposed half had faded to a pale cream. The onion skin samples hardly changed at all.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Turmeric is notorious for that, which is one reason it was never highly valued as a textile dye. What about the red cabbage?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That was the most interesting one chemically. In plain water, the dye bath was purple, but when we added vinegar, it turned pink, and with baking soda, it went green. So the colour of the fabric depended on what we added.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Right. The pigments in red cabbage are called anthocyanins, and they act as natural pH indicators, changing colour depending on how acidic or alkaline their surroundings are. You should definitely include an explanation of the chemistry behind that in your report, with the structures of the molecules if possible. It would strengthen the theoretical side considerably.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: Okay. One thing we're not happy with is how we measured the fading. We just compared the samples by eye and gave each one a score.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a fair concern, because judgements by eye are quite subjective. One option would be to photograph all the samples under identical lighting and then use image software to measure the colour values. That would give you numbers you could actually compare.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That's a great idea. We could do that next week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And when you write up, remember to say where your dye materials came from and how much you used of each, so that someone else could repeat the experiment.

listeningParts.title: The story of rubber
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a materials science course on the history and chemistry of rubber.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at a material that most of us use every day without giving it a second thought: rubber. It's in our car tyres, our shoes, our medical gloves and countless seals and hoses. Its history is a fascinating mix of chemistry, accident and global politics.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Natural rubber comes from latex, a milky white fluid produced by certain plants. By far the most important source is the rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis, which is native to the Amazon basin. When the bark is cut, latex slowly oozes out and can be collected in a cup, a process known as tapping. Chemically, rubber is a polymer, made up of very long chain molecules, and it's the ability of these tangled chains to stretch out and then spring back that gives rubber its elasticity.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The peoples of Mesoamerica were using rubber more than three thousand years ago. They famously made solid rubber balls for a ritual ball game, which astonished the Spanish when they arrived, since nothing in Europe bounced like that. Researchers have also shown that Mesoamerican craftspeople mixed latex with the juice of a particular vine, a type of morning glory, and that by changing the proportions they could make rubber that was either bouncier or more hard-wearing, depending on what it was to be used for.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Europeans first became aware of rubber after Columbus's voyages, but for a long time it was little more than a curiosity. In 1770, the English chemist Joseph Priestley noticed that a small piece of it could rub out pencil marks, which is how the material got its English name. But raw rubber had serious drawbacks. In hot weather, it became soft and sticky and smelled unpleasant, and in cold weather, it turned hard and brittle. Early waterproof coats and boots made from it were notoriously unreliable.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The breakthrough came from the American inventor Charles Goodyear, who spent years experimenting, often in great poverty. In 1839, he found that heating rubber with sulphur transformed it into a material that stayed elastic and strong over a wide range of temperatures. According to a popular story, he discovered this by accident when a mixture fell onto a hot stove, though the story may have been improved in the retelling. The process became known as vulcanisation, after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. In Britain, Thomas Hancock obtained a patent for a similar process shortly before Goodyear's American patent was granted, and Goodyear, sadly, died heavily in debt.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So what does the sulphur actually do? It forms short bridges between neighbouring polymer chains. These bridges, which chemists call cross-links, stop the chains from sliding past one another permanently, so the rubber returns to its original shape after being stretched, instead of slowly flowing like a very thick liquid. The more cross-links there are, the harder the rubber becomes, and with a very large amount of sulphur, you get a hard, rigid material that was once used for things like combs and bowling balls.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Vulcanised rubber, combined with the invention of the air-filled tyre and later the motor car, created enormous demand. At first, almost all of it came from wild trees in the Amazon, and the trade made a few people extremely rich, while the workers who collected the latex were often brutally exploited. Then, in 1876, the Englishman Henry Wickham shipped tens of thousands of rubber seeds from Brazil to Kew Gardens in London. The seedlings that grew there were sent to British colonies in Asia, and within a few decades, huge plantations in Southeast Asia had replaced Brazil as the world's main source.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Interestingly, plantations have never succeeded in the Amazon itself, largely because of a fungal disease called South American leaf blight, which spreads rapidly when rubber trees are planted close together. That's still true today, and the leading producers are countries such as Thailand and Indonesia.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Dependence on Asian plantations became a serious problem during the Second World War, when Japan occupied the main rubber-growing regions and cut off supplies to the Allies. In response, the United States built an enormous synthetic rubber industry in just a few years. Synthetic rubbers are made from chemicals obtained from oil, and today they account for roughly half of all the rubber used in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, natural rubber hasn't been replaced. It still performs better in some demanding applications, for example the tyres of aircraft and heavy trucks, which have to cope with very high loads and heat. Next week, we'll look at the environmental questions this raises, including the problem of recycling the billions of tyres that are thrown away.

readingPassages.title: The remarkable history of glass
paragraphs: Glass is so much a part of modern life that it rarely attracts attention. We look through it, drink from it and cook in it, and through the optical fibres that carry internet data across the oceans, we even communicate by means of it. Yet glass is a puzzling substance. It is hard and brittle like a solid, but its internal structure resembles that of a liquid, and for thousands of years people made and used it without having any real understanding of why it behaved as it did.

Long before anyone learned to make glass, nature was producing it. When lava from a volcano cools very rapidly, its atoms have no time to arrange themselves into crystals, and the result is obsidian, a dark volcanic glass. Because it breaks into pieces with extremely sharp edges, obsidian was highly prized by prehistoric peoples for knives and arrowheads, and it was traded over remarkably long distances. Natural glass can also form when lightning strikes sand, melting it into fragile, branching tubes known as fulgurites.

How humans first came to make glass is uncertain. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder told a story of merchants who, camping on a beach, rested their cooking pots on blocks of natron, a natural soda, and found next morning that the fire had fused the sand and soda into glass. Modern historians generally doubt this account, since an open fire would hardly have reached the necessary temperature. What is known is that the earliest manufactured glass objects, mostly beads, come from Mesopotamia and date back more than four thousand years. The first glass vessels were produced by a laborious technique called core-forming, in which molten glass was wound around a core of clay and dung that was scraped out once the glass had cooled.

The great turning point came in the first century BCE, when craftsmen somewhere on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean discovered that molten glass could be inflated by blowing through a hollow tube. Glassblowing allowed vessels to be made in minutes rather than days, and as the technique spread through the Roman Empire, glass changed from a luxury into an everyday material. Cups, bottles and storage jars became common, and the Romans even began to set small panes of glass in windows, although this early window glass was thick, bubbly and far from transparent.

The chemistry of glass explains many of the challenges early glassmakers faced. Pure silica, the main component of sand, melts only at temperatures above 1,700 degrees Celsius, far beyond the reach of ancient furnaces. Adding soda acts as a flux, lowering the melting point considerably, but glass made only of silica and soda slowly dissolves in water. The solution was to add lime, obtained from limestone or shells, which makes the glass chemically stable. This combination, known as soda-lime glass, still accounts for the great majority of the glass made today, from bottles to windows. In all these glasses, the atoms are arranged randomly rather than in a regular pattern, which is why scientists describe glass as an amorphous solid.

This unusual structure has given rise to a persistent myth. Visitors to medieval churches are often told that the windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is really a very slow-moving liquid that has flowed downwards over the centuries. Calculations show, however, that at room temperature such flow would be undetectable even over billions of years. The real explanation lies in how the glass was made. Medieval window glass was often produced by spinning molten glass into a large disc, which was uneven in thickness, and glaziers usually, though not always, placed the heavier edge at the bottom. Indeed, some old windows have their thicker edge at the top.

During the Middle Ages, Venice became the centre of European glassmaking. In 1291, the city's glassmakers were ordered to move their furnaces to the nearby island of Murano, partly because of the risk of fire spreading through the crowded city. The craftsmen were valued so highly that they were forbidden to leave the republic, for fear that they would take their secrets with them. In the fifteenth century, Venetian workshops developed cristallo, an exceptionally clear glass. Two centuries later in England, George Ravenscroft found that adding lead oxide produced a heavy, brilliant glass, now called lead crystal, which was ideal for cutting into decorative patterns.

Making large, flat sheets remained difficult and expensive until the twentieth century. Plate glass had to be ground and polished on both sides, a slow process that wasted much of the material. In the 1950s, Alastair Pilkington and his colleagues at the British company Pilkington Brothers developed the float process, announced in 1959, in which molten glass is poured onto a bath of molten tin. The glass spreads out and floats on the metal, producing a perfectly smooth, flat surface on both sides without polishing. Most of the world's flat glass is now made in this way. Glass also has an environmental advantage: it can be recycled repeatedly without losing quality, and crushed recycled glass melts at a lower temperature than raw materials, saving considerable energy.

readingPassages.title: The age of plastic
paragraphs: Few materials have transformed everyday life as rapidly as plastics. Chemically, plastics are polymers, substances made of extremely long molecules in which small units called monomers are joined together in chains that may contain thousands of links; the word comes from the Greek for 'many parts'. Global production has risen from around two million tonnes in 1950 to more than four hundred million tonnes a year today, and it is now difficult to find a manufactured object that contains no plastic at all.

Polymers themselves are not new. Nature produces them in abundance, and for centuries people shaped materials such as horn, tortoiseshell, natural rubber and shellac, a resin secreted by the lac insect, into combs, buttons and ornaments. These materials, however, were available only in limited quantities, and some, such as ivory, came at a heavy cost to the animals that supplied them. As industrial societies grew, demand far outstripped supply, and inventors began searching for substitutes.

The first steps were taken using plant material. In 1862, the British inventor Alexander Parkes displayed Parkesine, a mouldable material made from cellulose, at the International Exhibition in London, but his business failed within a few years. In the United States, John Wesley Hyatt developed celluloid, reportedly encouraged by a prize offered for a substitute for ivory in billiard balls. Celluloid proved useful for many purposes, most famously photographic and cinema film, despite being highly flammable, a property that caused numerous fires in early cinemas.

The first fully synthetic plastic, made entirely from chemicals rather than modified natural substances, was invented in 1907 by Leo Baekeland, a Belgian-born chemist working in New York. Bakelite, produced by reacting phenol with formaldehyde, could be moulded into almost any shape, and once it had set under heat and pressure, it could not be melted again. Because it did not conduct electricity and resisted heat, it was ideal for telephones, radio cases and electrical plugs, and its makers promoted it as the material of a thousand uses.

Several important plastics were discovered by accident. In 1933, Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson, chemists at the British company ICI, were conducting high-pressure experiments with ethylene gas when they found a white, waxy solid in their apparatus: polyethylene. Light, flexible and an excellent electrical insulator, it became vital during the Second World War for insulating the cables of radar equipment. At around the same time, Wallace Carothers at the American company DuPont produced nylon, which was launched in women's stockings and sold in vast quantities until wartime needs diverted it to parachutes and ropes.

Chemists divide plastics into two broad families. Thermoplastics, which include polyethylene, PET and PVC, soften when heated and harden again as they cool, so in principle they can be melted down and reshaped many times. Thermosets, such as Bakelite and epoxy resins, form a rigid network of chemical bonds as they set, and cannot be remelted. Even thermoplastics, however, are seldom easy to recycle, because most products contain additives, such as colourings, softeners and flame retardants, and many items combine several types of plastic that must be separated before they can be processed.

The scale of the resulting waste problem was quantified in a widely cited study published in 2017 by the American researchers Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law. They estimated that around 8.3 billion tonnes of plastic had been produced up to 2015, and that of the plastic that had become waste, only about nine per cent had been recycled, while around twelve per cent had been burned and the rest had accumulated in landfill sites or the natural environment. Because plastics break down extremely slowly, much of this material persists as fragments, and microplastics, pieces smaller than five millimetres, have now been found from Arctic sea ice to the deepest ocean sediments.

Solutions are being pursued on several fronts, but none is straightforward. Mechanical recycling usually reduces the quality of the material, so that drinks bottles, for instance, are often turned into fibres for clothing rather than into new bottles. Chemical recycling, which breaks polymers back down into monomers, could in theory produce plastic as good as new, but it remains expensive and energy-intensive. Bioplastics made from plant sources are another option, yet many of them break down only under the high temperatures of industrial composting facilities and persist in the sea much like conventional plastics. Meanwhile, the benefits of plastics, from lighter vehicles that use less fuel to sterile medical equipment, mean that simply abandoning them is not a realistic option.

readingPassages.title: Colour from coal tar
paragraphs: Until the middle of the nineteenth century, every dye in the world came from a plant, an animal or a mineral. Blue was obtained from indigo plants in India or from woad in Europe, red from the roots of the madder plant, and crimson from cochineal, an insect harvested in the Americas. Some colours were extraordinarily costly. Tyrian purple, extracted from sea snails, required thousands of snails to produce a single gram of dye, and for centuries it was reserved for emperors and the highest officials.

This situation was transformed by an eighteen-year-old student. In 1856, William Henry Perkin was working as an assistant to August Wilhelm von Hofmann at the Royal College of Chemistry in London. Hofmann had suggested that quinine, the only effective treatment for malaria and then obtained at great expense from the bark of the cinchona tree, might be made from chemicals found in coal tar, a waste product of the gas industry. During the Easter holiday, in a makeshift laboratory at home, Perkin attempted the synthesis. He failed to make quinine, obtaining instead a black sludge, but when he dissolved it in alcohol, it produced a brilliant purple solution that dyed silk. It is often called a lucky accident, but in my view that does Perkin an injustice; many chemists would simply have thrown the sludge away.

Against Hofmann's advice, Perkin left the college, patented his dye and, with money from his father, built a factory at Greenford, near London. The difficulties were considerable: the raw materials had to be manufactured in quantities never attempted before, and traditional dyers had to be persuaded to use an unfamiliar product. Fashion came to his rescue. The colour, soon known as mauve, became highly fashionable after it was adopted by Empress Eugénie of France and Queen Victoria, and Perkin became a wealthy man while still in his twenties.

Perkin's success set off a wave of research, but it was Germany, rather than Britain, that turned synthetic dyes into a great industry. Companies such as BASF, Bayer and Hoechst were founded in the 1860s and employed university-trained chemists on a scale unknown elsewhere. In 1868, Carl Graebe and Carl Liebermann produced alizarin, the red colouring of madder, the first time a natural dye had been made synthetically, and within a few decades madder cultivation in Europe had almost disappeared. Adolf von Baeyer worked out how to synthesise indigo, and after many years of development BASF began selling synthetic indigo in 1897, with devastating consequences for India's indigo exports. By the early twentieth century, German firms made the great majority of the world's dyes. I would argue that this dominance owed less to individual genius than to the close links that Germany built between its universities and its companies.

The new dyes also had unexpected consequences for medicine. The German scientist Paul Ehrlich noticed that certain dyes stained some types of cell and microbe but not others, and reasoned that a chemical might be found that would attack disease-causing organisms while leaving the body's own cells unharmed. This idea of a 'magic bullet' led in 1910 to Salvarsan, the first effective treatment for syphilis. In the 1930s, Gerhard Domagk, working for Bayer, discovered that a red dye called Prontosil could cure bacterial infections in mice, leading to the sulphonamide drugs, the first widely used antibacterial medicines.

The industry's achievements, however, came at a cost. Dye factories discharged their waste directly into rivers, and in some cases, the colour of a river downstream depended on what was being produced that day. Workers handling certain chemicals used in dye production suffered unusually high rates of bladder cancer, a link first reported in the 1890s. Today, much textile dyeing takes place in countries where environmental regulation is weak, and according to an often-quoted estimate, the dyeing and treatment of textiles may be responsible for up to a fifth of industrial water pollution worldwide.

Given this record, it is not surprising that natural dyes are enjoying a revival among designers and consumers. In my view, however, a large-scale return to natural dyes is neither possible nor desirable. Growing enough plants to colour the world's clothing would require vast areas of farmland, natural colours are often inconsistent and prone to fading, and many traditional methods depend on metal salts as mordants, some of which are themselves toxic. Natural, in short, is not automatically harmless.

A more promising path lies in making synthetic dyeing cleaner. Factories can treat and reuse their water, chemists are designing dyes that bind more completely to fibres so that less is washed away, and some companies are experimenting with dyeing methods that use carbon dioxide under pressure instead of water. Such technologies are not yet widespread, and they will require investment and regulation to succeed. Nevertheless, I believe Perkin's legacy is best honoured not by turning our backs on chemistry but by applying it more responsibly.

writingTask1.title: Recycling glass bottles
writingTask1.instructions: The diagram below shows how used glass bottles are recycled to make new bottles. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
processSteps: Used bottles are collected from bottle banks and household bins
Bottles are taken to a treatment plant and sorted by colour
Labels, caps and other contaminants are removed
Glass is crushed into small pieces called cullet
Cullet is mixed with sand, soda ash and limestone
The mixture is melted in a furnace at about 1,500°C
Molten glass is shaped into new bottles in moulds
New bottles are cooled slowly, inspected and sent to drinks companies
keyOverviewPoints: The process is cyclical, with eight stages from collection to the delivery of new bottles.
It combines sorting and cleaning stages with melting and moulding at high temperature.
